snippet.title: Hands-on with Minecraft's raytracing beta: So shiny
snippet.description:
Minecraft is on it's way to receiving raytraced graphics support, and we took a look at it's new beta. Adding high-quality realistic lighting to a game famous for it's chunky blocky graphics may be a strange choice, but the results are incredible. It's still pretty hard on the GPU, though we got good frame-rates on a 2080 ti with DLSS enabled.

snippet.title: Quibi review: Who needs this?
snippet.description:
We've already seen Disney Plus and Apple TV launch in the past twelve months, and HBO Max will be joining them soon. But into this crowded streaming landscape has stepped Quibi, a new video streaming service that's putting mobile first.

Except we're not sure why. Despite being founded by heavyweight Hollywood executives, and boasting more than $1.7 billion dollars in funding, we're not sure why Quibi exists. It's built around short-form (under 10 minute) videos that you can watch on your phone (and ONLY on your phone). Its selling point is Turnstyle, a technology that no one was asking for, and some shows are fine, but hardly better than what's on Netflix, Hulu, or even YouTube. So we're left asking, who is this for?

snippet.title: My love/hate relationship with streaming movies early at home
snippet.description:
With most of the world encouraged to stay inside, movie studios are pushing films straight to VOD and streaming. Even recent releases like Invisible Man, Emma, and Pixar's Onward are being rushed onto platform like Amazon, Vudu, an iTunes.

Direct-to-video used to be reserved for films of lower budget (or quality) but in the age of streaming, more films are already skipping theaters to go straight online. With theaters now closed for weeks or months, is this going to be the new default?

snippet.title: Hunting coronavirus protein with the biggest supercomputer on Earth | Upscaled Mini
snippet.description:
How many computers working together would you need to be faster than the world's best supercomputer? This week, the distributing computing project Folding at Home found out. Their software uses volunteer computers to analyze proteins, and once they turned their attention to the coronavirus, they saw a massive increase in new users. For the moment,their network has become the fastest supercomputer on Earth. Hopefully their results will help us understand the virus and better combat COVID-19. If you're looking for another project to support, also consider Rosetta, which does similar protein analysis.
